title: Exercise Helps the Aging Brain Clear Toxic Waste, New Research Shows
excerpt: A review published in Trends in Neurosciences finds that physical activity strengthens the brain's glymphatic system, its built-in cleanup mechanism that removes harmful proteins linked to dementia.
body:
• Regular exercise enhances the brain's glymphatic system, which flushes out metabolic waste including proteins linked to Alzheimer's disease
  • The review, published in Trends in Neurosciences, synthesised animal and human research showing exercise improves multiple processes involved in brain waste clearance
  • Benefits include reduced blood pressure, improved sleep quality and enhanced deep-sleep activity associated with brain cleanup
  • More than 10 million people are diagnosed with dementia worldwide each year, and no cure currently exists

Regular physical exercise may help the aging brain "take out the trash" by strengthening a cleanup system that removes toxic waste products, according to a review led by Victoria University researchers and published in Trends in Neurosciences.

The review examined existing animal and human research on the glymphatic system — a recently discovered brain clearance pathway that removes metabolic waste, including harmful proteins associated with Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative conditions.

How the Brain's Cleanup System Works

Discovered in 2012, the glymphatic system works primarily during sleep. Cerebrospinal fluid flows along channels surrounding blood vessels in the brain, flushing out waste products including beta-amyloid and tau — proteins that accumulate in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease.

The system relies on a water channel protein called aquaporin-4 (AQP4), located on astrocytes — support cells that help maintain the brain's environment. When AQP4 is properly positioned, fluid moves efficiently through the brain. When it is not, waste accumulates.

Exercise Strengthens the System

The Victoria University review, led by Dr. James Broatch, found that exercise improves several biological processes critical to glymphatic function:

  • Reduces blood pressure and vascular stiffness, improving fluid flow
  • Improves neuronal activation in the brain
  • Reduces brain inflammation
  • Lowers resting norepinephrine levels
  • Improves sleep quality, particularly deep-sleep stages linked to brain waste clearance

In animal studies, voluntary wheel running increased glymphatic fluid flow by more than twofold in young mice. Six weeks of exercise in aged mice reduced inflammatory activation of brain support cells, improving AQP4 positioning and accelerating waste drainage.

"If we don't have opportunities for the brain to essentially clean out the junk from the day, we know that buildup is damaging, especially as we age. Sleep is more crucial than ever to play this role, but the irony is, good-quality sleep can often be harder to get as we get older. This study asked, what if exercise could support that process?"

— Dr. James Broatch, Victoria University

Human Evidence Growing

The evidence extends beyond animal models. A study published in Nature Communications showed that a 12-week structured exercise programme significantly enhanced both glymphatic and meningeal lymphatic vessel flow in human participants, compared to a shorter exercise protocol. These clearance systems work together to remove waste from the brain.

The exercise-induced improvements in cerebral blood flow, arterial flexibility and sleep quality may all contribute indirectly to optimising the brain's waste clearance environment.

Why This Matters

With more than 10 million people diagnosed with dementia worldwide each year and no cure on the horizon, understanding how lifestyle factors protect the brain is increasingly urgent. The glymphatic system offers a potential mechanism explaining exercise's well-documented cognitive benefits.

"If nothing else, this is yet another reminder that regular movement — especially the type that lifts your heart rate — is so important for every part of your health. The earlier we can develop these good habits, the better as we age," Broatch said.

The research team acknowledged that questions remain about the optimal type, intensity and duration of exercise for maximising glymphatic benefits, and whether exercise can help people who are already in cognitive decline. Further studies addressing these gaps are currently underway.
